stature.source: typical: an estimate for open headland trees; tall: Gymnosperm Database, to about 25 m; record: a 48 m tree in San Francisco (Gymnosperm Database; planted), the US champion by points is 31.1 m with a 33.8 m spread near Pescadero; read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values, no photographs measured: Gymnosperm Database, crown broad-spreading and fairly sparse with major limbs near the base, broader on exposed headlands, more upright in shelter; the champion's spread (33.8 m) exceeds its height (31.1 m)

young.note: a dense, upright, pyramidal young tree of dark green sprays, branches to the ground

old-growth.note: an old headland tree: a short massive trunk splitting into heavy, twisting limbs under a broad, flat, wind-sheared table of foliage, much wider than tall

description: The cypress of the Monterey headlands, a pyramid when young and later a broad, flat-topped, wind-carved crown on a few massive twisting limbs. Its dense foliage of tiny scale leaves is a dark, slightly bronze green and smells of lemon when crushed.

season_notes.winter: Storm winds off the sea shear the crown flat and lean it away from the water.
season_notes.spring: Fresh tips lighten the dark foliage and yellow pollen sheds.
season_notes.summer: Fog wraps the headland trees and beads on the scale leaves.
season_notes.fall: Round woody cones the size of walnuts hang closed in clusters, some opening in warm spells.

range.where: native only at Cypress Point and Point Lobos near Carmel; planted and wind-shaped on the San Francisco and Marin headlands

notes: Grown from incense cedar (same family, scale foliage in sprays, fibrous bark) but with almost everything changed: a short trunk that splits low into three heavy ascending limbs, long limbs reaching a broad, flat-topped crown (W/H 1.35, old trees wider), darker foliage and a grey-brown fibrous bark in place of incense cedar's cinnamon. The high asymmetry stands for the wind-shear of headland trees; what the generator cannot express is the true windward lean and the sheared, sloping top that points away from the sea (it needs a wind direction per tile), the bleached dead limbs on the weather side, and the orange alga that coats the branches at Point Lobos. Doubt: like Monterey pine, the species is native only near Carmel (Gymnosperm Database); the San Francisco cypresses are planted, so a humanless San Francisco would not have them unless the game keeps naturalised stands. Wildlife records read were thin: ravens and hawks use the big crowns as perches and nest sites (general knowledge, not from a source read); seed eaters are a guess from the squirrel's habits.
